QF.id: SIA Case Studies on SAS Standards_72

question.text: Under SAS-1300 the chief LIMITATION of E-Diksha-style financial-literacy programmes is that:

answer.text: Behavioural change is hard to sustain — knowledge gain at training may not translate into long-term behaviour; the SIA must measure 6-12 month post-training behaviour as the outcome, not immediate session satisfaction

explanation.text: The Logic: Knowledge gained at a training session typically decays rapidly. Whether learners convert that knowledge into sustained behaviour over the following months is the central methodological question for any financial-literacy programme. A defensible outcome measure therefore tracks behaviour 6-12 months after training, not just immediate session satisfaction or knowledge gain on the training day. The Trap: Options A, C and D — sessions being boring, trainers unavailable, or jargon being complex — are operational programme issues, not the core methodological limitation of attributing sustained behaviour change to a literacy intervention. Note: The cited SIA workbook describes E-Diksha objectives and lists limitations such as participants' inability to communicate learnings, limited accurate non-formal-source data, and attribution difficulty, but it does not specifically state a 6-12 month sustained behavioural-change measurement requirement. The framing above reflects general financial-literacy evaluation practice (OECD/RBI-style) rather than a workbook-page citation.
